title: Speaking Early

learn.summary: Input builds comprehension, but Merrill Swain's output hypothesis showed speaking does unique work: producing language forces you to notice exactly what you cannot yet say. You do not need to speak on day one, but by the time you know a few hundred words, regular low-stakes speaking — a tutor, an exchange partner, or talking to yourself — accelerates everything. Comfort with sounding bad is the actual skill.

do: Book one 30-minute conversation session (tutor or exchange partner) for this week and show up, whatever your level.

children.title: Shadowing

learn.summary: Shadowing — repeating native audio aloud in near-real time, like a simultaneous interpreter — was popularized for language learning by polyglot linguist Alexander Arguelles and builds pronunciation, prosody, and speech speed at once. Start with short, clearly spoken clips you already understand; echo a half-second behind the speaker. Ten focused minutes a day audibly changes your accent within weeks.

do: Shadow the same 2-minute native audio clip daily for 5 days, recording yourself on day 1 and day 5 to compare.

children.title: Tutors & Exchanges

learn.summary: Online tutoring platforms like iTalki made hour-long one-on-one practice with native speakers cheap and abundant; language exchanges (tandems) trade half your language for half of theirs, for free. A tutor's job at your stage is mostly conversation partner plus error-noticer — you do not need a certified teacher for that, and 'community tutors' cost less. Weekly scheduled sessions create the deadline that makes you study.

do: Set up a recurring weekly tutor or tandem session and keep it for 4 consecutive weeks before judging progress.

children.title: Scripts for Real Situations

learn.summary: Most real-life exchanges are predictable: ordering, greeting, buying, asking directions, introducing yourself. Write short scripts for your top situations — including the replies you are likely to hear — and drill them to automaticity. This 'island of competence' approach gives you fluent-feeling wins months before you are generally fluent, and each script becomes a scaffold you improvise around.

do: Write and memorize scripts for your 3 most likely real situations, then use at least one in a live session this week.

children.title: Mistakes as Data

learn.summary: Krashen's affective filter hypothesis says anxiety measurably suppresses acquisition — the embarrassed learner takes in less. The reframe that works: every mistake in conversation is a free diagnostic you could not have gotten alone, and native speakers overwhelmingly respond to effort with goodwill, not judgment. Ask partners to correct only errors that impede understanding; total correction kills flow.

do: In your next session, deliberately attempt 3 constructions you are unsure of, and add the corrections to your error log.
